ak_lower_crack_in_the_woods.blurb: Lower Crack in the Woods is the right-hand branch of a small, quiet pair of cliffs tucked beside the Seward Highway south of Anchorage. Eight routes are packed in here, mostly gear climbs with a couple of bolted lines and one top-rope. The range runs from easy ground up to low 5.11, with several moderate crack and face lines at 5.7 that suit climbers stepping onto natural protection. The walls are short, set back under trees, and reached by a short walk through the woods along a creek, where prickly devil's club is something to avoid. The setting is usually calmer and less windy than the roadside, but bugs can be fierce, so bring repellent.

ak_lower_wall.blurb: Lower Wall is the lower of two cliffs at the small 43 Mile crag along the Richardson Highway, roughly 43 miles from Valdez. It sits right above the old highway alignment, so the walk to it is brief, and it is the wall that grabs your attention first. Eight routes are catalogued here, all with a mountain-style feel, from moderate up to low 5.11, with most of the weight in the 5.10 range. The wall loses sun earlier in the day than its neighbours. Loose rock is a theme across the crag, so wear a helmet and test holds. It makes a handy dry-weather fallback when Valdez itself is socked in by rain.

ak_northwest_passage.blurb: Northwest Passage is a shaded cliff on the Seward Highway corridor south of Anchorage, near the pullout just past Beluga Point. It holds eight routes, mostly bolted lines with one gear route and a top-rope, and the grades center on 5.10 with a few at 5.11 and a handful of easier lines. The cliff is reached by a steep hike up a scree field from a small, hard-to-spot trail across from the pullout, and the path needs work, so expect a somewhat tough approach. Rock along this corridor is generally loose and chossy, so a helmet is essential, and the shade keeps it cool for summer days.

ak_near_tors_lizard_s_eye.blurb: Lizard's Eye is a granite wall among the Granite Tors, a set of buttresses above tree line in the hills near Fairbanks and Chena Hot Springs. It is regarded as the busiest crag out there. Eight routes up to about 60 feet are mostly gear-protected, with one top-rope line, ranging from easy fifth class to low 5.11 with a good number around 5.9 and 5.10. Lightly climbed lines are gritty and covered in lichen, while the popular ones have cleaned up. The wall runs north to south. It is a remote backcountry outing: the trail loops for hours to reach the first outcrop, and the wall is a short distance beyond it.

ak_throne_the.blurb: The Throne is a large peak of about 7,390 feet in Little Switzerland, within Denali National Park, and it is a serious alpine objective. Climbers fly from Talkeetna onto the Pika Glacier and camp below the walls. Routes are long multi-pitch lines of around 10 to 12 pitches, with a steep west face carrying a huge roof and scar, plus a south-side gully system used for descending. Grades on the catalogued routes center on 5.10 and run from moderate to low 5.11 and a bit harder. Expect cracks, offwidths, some moss and lichen, and wet sections, with snow slopes near the summit.

ak_pandemic_area.blurb: Pandemic Area is the most developed sector of the Tanana River Bluffs, a riverside granite cliff line near Fairbanks, with views toward the Hayes Range. Eight routes, mostly gear climbs with a couple of bolted lines, ranging from 5.8 to the 5.11 range, follow cracks of every size from fingers to offwidth. It faces south, so it sees sun all day, with a breeze coming off the river. Rock can be loose in places, though every line now has an anchor. A long walk through boggy forest gets you there, or you can paddle down the Tanana.
ak_pandemic_area.parking_note: Leave the car at the Birch Lake pullout beside the Richardson Highway, then cross the road to where two trees are tied with pink flagging.
ak_pandemic_area.approach: From the Birch Lake pullout, follow the pink-flagged trail for roughly 2.5 miles through forest, including a swampy stretch of black spruce. Plan on a little over an hour. The alternative is floating the Tanana by boat.
